title: Where you hold it
hookLine: stress often lands in the jaw, shoulders or belly

cards: Where are your shoulders right now? Don't change anything first. Are they sitting low and easy, or have they crept up toward your ears?

Your teeth: touching, or pressed together? Your belly: soft, or pulled in like you're bracing for a hit? Often at least one of them turns out to be on duty, holding something, for no reason anyone could name.
That's what yesterday's scan was quietly turning up. Today gets specific.

teach.b: When the body senses a threat, it gets ready.
In a 1915 book, the American physiologist Walter Cannon described that readiness for fighting or for flight, and fight or flight is the name that stuck.
The heart speeds up, breathing quickens, and muscles tighten, ready to strike or run. That's useful if there's a bear.
The trouble is that a hard email, a traffic jam or a tense dinner can set off a smaller version of the same thing, with nothing to strike and nowhere to run.
So the tension just stays, and it tends to settle in the same few places. The jaw: some people clench their teeth when stressed, often without knowing, some even in their sleep.
The shoulders: they rise and round forward, a little like a turtle pulling in. The belly: the muscles brace, and breathing moves up into the chest.
In 1929, a Chicago doctor named Edmund Jacobson published a book called Progressive Relaxation.
His discovery was simple: people often can't feel how tense a muscle is until they first tighten it on purpose, and then let go.

The contrast teaches the body what soft feels like. None of this needs a teacher or a mat, just a habit of checking. These three places are where a hard day tends to show, and you can let them go, one muscle at a time.

how: Some people use progressive muscle relaxation, tensing and then releasing each muscle group in turn, and relaxation courses often teach a quick check of the jaw, shoulders and belly during the day.

games.q: you can't tell if your shoulders are tense. what does Jacobson's method say to do?
o: ignore it; if you can't feel it, it's fine.
tighten them on purpose, then let go.
stretch as hard as you can.
games.why: tighten on purpose, hold, and let go. the contrast teaches the body what soft feels like.

practice: Let your teeth part a little, lips closed, tongue resting. Lift your shoulders toward your ears on purpose, hold for a breath, let them fall and feel the difference, then once more.
Last, let the belly go soft and the breath drop down into it, and each time something tightens, notice, and let it down again.

wordCard.voice: Jacobson. The doctor who found that tensing a muscle on purpose, then letting go, teaches the body what soft feels like. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: let the shoulders down. Soft is something the body can learn. Rest easy; see you tomorrow.
